nameStory: The snakefish gets its name from its elongated, cylindrical body that resembles a snake more than a typical fish. Also called the blunt-nose lizardfish, it belongs to a family where many species have that distinctive reptilian look with their long bodies and pointed snouts.
description: The snakefish is an unusual-looking predatory fish with an elongated, snake-like body that can grow up to 16 inches long. It has a somewhat flattened head with a blunt snout and a mouth full of sharp teeth designed for catching smaller fish. This Atlantic Ocean species is rarely seen in New England waters, making any encounter quite special. Its streamlined body and bottom-dwelling habits make it well-adapted for ambush hunting.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Long, cylindrical body that feels firm and muscular, resembling a snake more than a typical fish - the body tapers gradually from head to tail

idTips.label: Mouth
idTips.description: Large mouth with prominent sharp teeth that you can easily see even when the mouth is closed - feels rough if you run your finger along the jaw

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Can reach up to 16 inches in length, making it a substantial fish when fully grown - most specimens you'll encounter are smaller

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Typically brownish or grayish with mottled patterns that help it blend with sandy or rocky bottom - colors may appear duller when out of water

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Large pectoral fins and a distinctive dorsal fin positioned relatively far forward on the body - fins feel sturdy and well-developed

habitat: Snakefish are extremely rare visitors to New England waters, typically found in deeper offshore Atlantic waters rather than coastal areas. When they do appear, it's usually in deeper waters beyond the continental shelf where they prefer sandy or muddy bottoms for ambush hunting.

seasonality.spring: Most likely time to encounter this rare species in New England waters, coinciding with one of their spawning periods from February to April when they may move into different areas.
seasonality.summer: Less likely to be seen during summer months as they retreat to deeper, cooler waters offshore.
seasonality.fall: Another potential time for sightings from August to October during their second spawning season, though still extremely uncommon in our region.
seasonality.winter: Rarely encountered as they remain in deeper offshore waters during the coldest months.

funFact: Snakefish have two distinct spawning seasons per year - one in spring and another in fall - which scientists believe helps them adapt to different environmental conditions and maximize their reproductive success!
confusionNotes: With only 11 recorded observations in New England, you're unlikely to confuse this with anything else simply because it's so rare! If you think you've found one, the snake-like body shape and large mouth with visible teeth should confirm it's not a typical New England fish.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'snakefish,' this species is also known as the blunt-nose lizardfish, showing how common names can vary regionally. The 'lizardfish' name refers to the entire family (Synodontidae), while 'snakefish' specifically describes this species' body shape.
compareHints: The snakefish is the only member of its genus (Trachinocephalus) found in New England waters. Compared to other lizardfish family members, it has a more blunt snout rather than a pointed one, and its body tends to be more robust and cylindrical. The blunt nose is actually its most distinguishing feature from other similar-looking predatory fish.
